job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Omar Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty relaxed, honestly. I live with my parents in Lindenhof, and my dad's a machinist, so the house wakes at six whether I like it or not. I apply to startups and mid-size firms in the morning, then work on a side project, a simple sales dashboard that I'm trying to sell to local machine shops. I studied business analytics at Ostermark University and passed with an average result, no internship. I use AI tools every day, to write code, check my maths, even to plan my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it saves a bit of time and that's that. The tools I use already work, and nobody needs to panic or party. People will keep using them for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing much changes. I'd still be hunting, still working on my dashboard. I'm a bit impatient, because I know I can do the work, and I don't have a piece of paper from a firm to prove it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to about 15 places a week, and I'd tidy my project into a clean demo with real numbers from a machine shop. I'd also ask my dad's boss to let me look at their production data, with permission. And I'd publish a couple of short write-ups on how the dashboard works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, a bit bored. I'm not worried about money. I've got savings, no debt, and my parents don't charge me rent. I'd just like something to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've applied to a lot of places. Why do you think there's no offer yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that I've got nothing from a real firm on my CV. Firms say they want experience, and then nobody gives the first piece. The demo is my way round that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your first job to give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere I can learn from people who are better than me, and see how a real business uses data. Pay is secondary at first. I want a manager who explains things.

I'm **not worried** about money, with savings and no rent.

Ask my dad's boss for permission to look at **production data**.
Publish a couple of short **write-ups** on how the dashboard works.
feel: **Good**, a bit bored, with no money worry thanks to savings and no rent.

fieldNote: He is **relaxed and capable**, and his only itch is lack of proof from a real firm.
The dashboard is a **side-income** attempt and also a portfolio piece.
Secure cushion and plentiful openings justify calm.

steps.text: Polish the dashboard into a demo with real shop data
Publish short write-ups explaining the dashboard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's big but manageable, and the people who use the tools will do well. I'd tell friends to learn them now, because it's easier than learning later. I'd also say firms should keep hiring juniors, because who else becomes the seniors?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm in a decent spot. I code with AI every day, so I'm ahead of most graduates. The risk is that entry roles shrink and firms ask for two years of experience that nobody can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the dashboard harder, maybe 10 paying shop clients by next summer. I'd apply to firms that build with AI. And I'd learn one more tool each month, like workflow automation, to stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, a little excited. I like new tools, so a changing job market feels like a game I enjoy, even if it has rules I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your skills are the ones on that card. Does that feel like an advantage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Junior analysts who only know spreadsheets, customer service staff, anyone whose day is mostly writing or checking. People who can't adapt fast. My mum's school office is already using software that replaced a part-time role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is exposed most in a world like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. I'd say the people around me who don't use the tools should be learning them now. If I'm honest, I'm already assuming that gap will grow.

Mother's school office gives a real example of a role replaced.

steps.text: Sell the dashboard to 10 paying machine shops

Learn one new automation tool every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move quickly on support and rules, and that it isn't fair to leave it to firms. I'd say it online and to my parents' friends. I'd also say nobody should believe anyone who claims to know exactly how it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy but not terrified. If AI does most thinking work, my skills are less special, because everybody can use them. But I'm young, I've got savings, and I'd spot opportunities faster than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending slightly and save more. I'd focus the dashboard on something concrete that machine shops will pay for, like maintenance planning. And I'd take any decent job offer, including one that's hands-on. My dad could probably get me a trainee place at his workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, a little wired. Not scared in a way that stops me, but it's a lot to take in. I'd probably go for a long run and think it through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you doing the week the announcement lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a few people, my dad, my old lecturer, a friend who works at a startup. I'd read the actual announcements instead of the commentary. Then I'd make a plan with numbers, what I earn, what I spend, what I'd do if the money stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does being good with AI help or just delay things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps for a while, because I'm faster. After that it's just parity. I'd be one of a million people who know how to type a prompt, so I'd have to add something else, like knowing a specific trade.

say: We need to move quickly on **support and rules**, and it isn't fair to leave it to firms.
Nobody should trust anyone who claims to know how it ends.
think: I'd be **uneasy but not terrified**: my skills become less special if everybody can use AI.
I'm young, I have savings and I'd spot opportunities faster.
do: Focus the dashboard on **maintenance planning**, which machine shops will pay for.
Accept any decent offer, even hands-on, such as a **trainee place** at Dad's workshop.
feel: **Alert** and a bit wired, but not scared in a way that stops me.
S2.quote: I'd read the actual announcements instead of the commentary. Then I'd make a plan with numbers
fieldNote: Adaptable and **numbers-first**: his reflex is to make a plan, not panic.
He recognises that AI skill becomes **parity** rather than an edge.
Dad's workshop is a real hands-on fallback.

steps.text: Cut spending a little and save more each month
Pitch maintenance planning dashboards to machine shops
Accept a trainee place at my dad's workshop if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan sensibly. Governments should pilot retraining and income support now, and firms should explain how they plan to use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fairly relaxed. Five years is long enough to get a job, learn a business, and build something of my own. I'd probably spend the first year working and the next four building on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a role at a firm that uses data heavily, keep the dashboard as a side business, and save at least a third of my pay. I'd learn the basics of machine maintenance data so I'm not just a generic analyst. And I'd put a small amount in index funds monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Calm with a bit of drive. It feels like a countdown that gives me a reason to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What do you build in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd avoid putting all my money into AI companies. Everyone will think of that. I'd also avoid becoming too narrow, because tools change quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd avoid doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd just move the first steps forward by a few years and treat the first job as school.

say: Five years is enough to plan sensibly, so pilot **retraining** and income support now.
Firms should explain how they plan to use AI.
think: I'm **fairly relaxed**, since five years lets me get a job, learn a business and build my own thing.
do: Take a role at a **data-heavy firm** and keep the dashboard as a side business.
Save at least **a third** of my pay and invest monthly in index funds.
Learn the basics of **machine maintenance** data.
feel: **Calm** with some drive, and the countdown gives me a reason to work.
S3.quote: I'd avoid putting all my money into AI companies. Everyone will think of that.
fieldNote: He treats the five years as a **build period**, with a clear first-year-then-side structure.
Shows realism about **investing**: avoids the obvious AI bet.
Wants a niche, machine maintenance data, instead of generic analysis.

steps.text: Take a role at a data-heavy firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's plenty of time to do this properly, with paid retraining, clear rules and a real social plan. I'd say it's the first time people can prepare for a change this size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm excited. By 2036 I'd be 33, with a decade of experience and maybe my own small company. I'd be better placed than most to use AGI, not just fear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job, learn a real industry, and build the dashboard into a proper product. I'd save steadily, maybe buy a small flat by 30. I'd also keep studying, maybe a part-time master's in data science.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. Like looking at a big map and picking a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More of a chance, with some risk. The risk is that I get comfortable and don't move. With ten years, comfort is a bigger danger than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this feel like a threat or a chance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick one new thing each year, a skill, a field, a project. That way I'm never starting from nothing.

say: Ten years is plenty of time to do this properly, with **paid retraining** and a real social plan.
People can finally prepare for a change this size.
think: I'm **excited**: at 33 I'd have a decade of experience and maybe my own company.
I'd be better placed than most to use AGI, not just fear it.
do: Get a first job, learn a real **industry** and build the dashboard into a product.
Save steadily and aim for a small **flat** by 30.
Study part-time for a **data science** master's.
feel: **Calm and curious**, like looking at a big map and picking a route.
S4.quote: With ten years, comfort is a bigger danger than panic.
fieldNote: He sees **comfort**, not fear, as the risk, an unusually self-aware answer.
Plans one new skill a year to avoid **starting from nothing**.
Calm is earned: cushion, skills and adaptive habits.

steps.text: Learn a real industry in my first job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though only mildly. It's the one where there's no time to build anything before it changes. What would help is a quick path to a first job, so I can show real work, and clear rules so firms can't just drop all their juniors at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I've got every advantage, and I try to remember it. The same tools that help me could be scary for my friends who don't use them. Somebody should help them early.

headlineQuote: I've got every advantage, and I try to remember it.
portrait: Omar is a **23-year-old** business analytics graduate living with his machinist dad and mum, selling a sales dashboard to machine shops.
He is **centre**, practical and wary of both hype and doom.
He is **adaptive**, uses AI daily and sees himself ahead of peers.
His savings and skills keep him **calm** in most worlds and only uneasy when time runs out.
He sees comfort as his real risk and plans one new skill a year.
biggestWorry: His biggest worry is **AGI by 2028**, which leaves no time to build anything first.
whatWouldHelp: A quick path to a **first job**, clear rules on dropping juniors, and early help for friends who don't use AI.
